Insights into the Solvation Characteristics of Zwitterionic Deep Eutectic Solvents Using Multiple Polarity Scales
Nabeel Mujtaba Abbasi and Jared L. Anderson*
Cite This: Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2023, 62, 4084–4094 Read Online

ABSTRACT: Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) formed by mixing zwitterionic hydrogen bond acceptors (HBAs) with diol- and organic acid-based hydrogen bond donors (HBDs) are popular sustainable solvents. In addition to possessing an amphiphilic character, zwitterionic DESs offer unique solvation properties, unlike those composed of halide-containing HBAs. While all other popular classes of DESs have been investigated, no study has attempted to characterize the solvation characteristics of zwitter- ionic DESs. # 1. INTRODUCTION Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) are a popular choice of sustainable designer solvents employed in numerous scientific disciplines. 1,2 They are multicomponent fluids composed of a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) that interacts with a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) to yield eutectic mixtures possessing low melting points compared to the HBA and HBD alone. 3,4 While HBAs typically comprise tetraalkylammonium, phosphonium, imidazolium, and choline salts, the choice of HBDs can include organic acids, alcohols, amides, and carbohydrates. 5,6 DESs often possess desirable properties such as tunable viscosities, 7 low vapor pressures, 1,8 and ease of preparation, 1,9 and are preferentially employed in catalysis, 10,11 organic synthesis, 12 chemical separations, 13,14 and electrochemical applications. 15

Several classes of DESs have been established over the years, each possessing unique features and characteristics. ¹ Among these is the zwitterionic class of DESs that are predominantly composed of betaine [Bet] and L-carnitine [L-Car] salts employed as HBAs that offer lower cytotoxicity and do not generate undesirable side products compared to tetraalkylam- monium and choline salts. ¹⁶,¹⁷ It has been reported that halogen counterions can impart strong nucleophilic, alkaline, and oxidizing properties to halide-containing DESs that can severely corrode steel equipment employed in industrial plants. ¹⁷⁻¹⁹ More importantly, betaine is an industrially

obtained renewable resource formed as a byproduct of sugar production, while choline chloride [Ch⁺][Cl⁻] is acquired from fossil fuels.²⁰,²¹ Additionally, zwitterionic surfactants possess amphiphilic properties that allow them to form micelle-like assemblies and behave as hydrophilic and hydrophobic nanocontainers, properties and characteristics that are not achieved by other classes of DESs.²²,²³

Like all other classes of DESs, the polarity of zwitterionic DESs is strongly influenced by the type of HBA and HBD and/or their molar ratio.¹⁸,²⁷,²⁸ In an attempt to understand their molecular interactions, Abranches et al. studied the solid–liquid phase diagrams of betaine-based DESs and found that betaine possesses a charge imbalance and cannot establish strong ion– ion interactions with itself, unlike salts that possess counter-

ions.²⁰ Nevertheless, this study did not quantify the individual solvation interactions of these DESs. Conventionally, the solvation properties of DES systems have been investigated by studying their solvatochromic response to construct the betaine dye scale (EₜN).²⁹,³⁰ For example, an EₜN value of 0.36 was obtained for the [Ch⁺][Cl⁻]/glycolic acid DES compared to 0.79 for the [Ch⁺][Cl⁻]/malonic acid DES, thereby revealing their different solvation characteristics.³¹ Given that the EₜN scale is dependent on a single dye measurement, the Kamlet–Taft solvent parameters employ several solvatochromic probes and can measure the solvent's hydrogen bond donating ability (α), hydrogen bond accepting ability (β), and dipolarity/polarizability (π*).³¹,³² While the fluorescence-based probe approach was the first to characterize DES solvation proper-

For example, Kim and co-workers reported a statistically similar EᴛN value of 0.843 for the [Ch⁺][Cl⁻]/ urea/glycerol ternary DES system compared to 0.845 for the [Ch⁺][Cl⁻]/glycerol DES,³⁵ despite significant differences in their chemical structures. It has been concluded that the solvatochromic approach is insensitive to DES compositional changes due to their high polarity and is generally more reliable when the solvation properties from two different classes of DESs are compared.³¹,³²

In an attempt to enhance the sensitivity in characterizing DES solvation properties, inverse gas chromatography (IGC) has been recently employed to investigate solute-solvent interactions. 34,37 The chromatographic retention of a diverse variety of probe molecules is measured on DES stationary phases as a function of temperature in order to characterize and quantify their unique and simultaneous interactions with DESs. To date, popular DES combinations comprising tetraalkylammonium, phosphonium, and choline salts have been studied using both the IGC38 and the solvatochromic dye approaches. 30,31 While zwitterionic-based DESs composed of different classes of HBDs have been employed in several applications, no study has attempted to thoroughly characterize their individual solvation interactions. Currently, only a few zwitterionic DESs comprising N-oxide HBAs have been screened using the Nile red solvatochromic scale, 22 which only provides a single value for polarity and does not explain all types of unique interactions that the DESs are capable of undergoing. 2 Consequently, the solvation properties of zwitterionic DESs have not been investigated with either Kamlet–Taft parameters or IGC and, thus, cannot be compared to those of other DES classes.

In this study, zwitterionic DESs formed by mixing betaine-, L-carnitine, and sulfobetaine-based HBAs with alcohol- and organic acid-based HBDs were characterized for the first time using both the IGC and the solvatochromic dye method. The choice of HBA and HBD was carefully made to incorporate unique functional groups, such as phenyl and imidazolium substituents, while the molar ratio of HBD was systematically modulated to investigate the effect of the HBA/HBD ratio. Additionally, the solvation properties of DESs were bench- marked against neat HBDs that comprise them. Two different solvatochromic scales (Nile red polarity scale and the Kamlet- Taft solvent parameters) were employed to thoroughly characterize the solvation properties of all DESs using solvatochromic dyes. This study demonstrates the need to simultaneously employ multiple types of approaches and empirical polarity scales in order to fully characterize the solvation properties of complex DESs and is the first to thoroughly investigate subtle differences in solvation character- istics between surfactant-like and halide-containing DESs.

## 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION ### 2.1. Reagents, Materials, DES Preparation and Characterization. A comprehensive list of reagents and starting materials employed in this study is provided in the Supporting Information. All HBAs and HBDs were thoroughly dried for 48 h in a vacuum oven maintained at 25 °C prior to being employed in DES preparation using the grinding method. Precise quantities of reagents corresponding to

desired HBA/HBD ratios (see Figure 1) were weighed into a ceramic mortar using a clean spatula for zwitterionic salts and a transfer pipette for liquid HBDs. Contents of the mortar were ground together with a pestle until a homogeneous liquid was obtained. The newly prepared DESs were transferred into 20 mL glass vials and their purity was characterized using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy prior to further analysis; all ¹³C and ¹H NMR spectra are provided in the Supporting Information. The water content of each DES was found to be under 0.9 wt % (Table S1), as determined using a Metrohm 831 Karl Fischer coulometric titrator by measuring each sample in triplicate. Additionally, DES viscosity measurements were performed at 21.6 °C using an AMETEK Brookfield DV1 cone and plate viscometer (Middleborough, MA, USA) equipped with a CPA-51Z cone spindle and compared to halide-containing DESs that had similar chemical structures; data are provided in Table S2.

Thermal properties of DESs were characterized using a NETZSCH DSC 214 Polyma instrument (Selb, Germany). DESs that possessed a liquid consistency at room temperature were cooled from 40 to -120 °C at a rate of 10 °C min⁻¹ and subsequently heated to 80 °C at the same rate, while those that appeared as solids under ambient conditions were cooled to -65 °C at a rate of 10 °C min⁻¹ before reheating them to 200 °C at the same rate. DSC thermograms were analyzed using NETZSCH Proteus software to obtain the melting point and/or glass transition temperatures for all DESs, as shown in Table S3.

## 2.2. Solvatochromic Dye Measurements. To conduct polarity measurements for zwitterionic DESs using the solvatochromic approach, Nile red (NR), 4-nitroaniline (4-NA), and N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline (N,N-DENA) dyes were employed. 29 The NR and N,N-DENA dyes were dissolved in chloroform to prepare 0.01 M stock solutions, while 4-NA was solubilized in methanol at the same concentration. Dye solutions were stored under 4 °C, and 100 µL of each dye was pipetted into clean Eppendorf tubes. The solvent was evaporated by passing a gentle stream of nitrogen, leaving behind pure dyes as residues in the tubes. A 100 µL volume of DESs was placed into the Eppendorf tubes and thoroughly mixed with each of these dyes to fully solubilize them in the eutectic mixtures. A small volume of each DES/dye solution (20 µL) was transferred into a 96-well plate and analyzed using a Synergy H1 microplate reader (Biotek, Winooski, Vermont). Spectral scanning was performed between wavelengths of 300 and 700 nm in 1 nm increments. The maximum absorption wavelength (λmax) was recorded for each dye, and representative UV–Vis spectra can be found in Figure S1 of the Supporting Information.

## 2.3. DES Chromatographic Column Preparation and Characterization. DESs were employed as GC stationary phases using the static method of column preparation. A 32 mg mass of each DES was placed inside a 20 mL glass vial and dissolved in a mixture of dichloromethane/methanol (up to 5% methanol) to prepare DES coating solutions at a concentration of 0.32% w/v. Five-meter segments of deactivated fused-silica capillary were filled with DES coating solutions and sealed at one end using a metal clamp. The other end was connected to a vacuum and placed inside a water bath maintained at 40 °C. The solvent was steadily evaporated, and the DESs were coated onto the inner walls of the silica capillary. All DESs were coated as a uniform film with a thickness of 0.20 μm.39

## 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES), which are perceived to be the least toxic and most sustainable class of DESs, can be categorized into ionic and non-ionic. While non-ionic NADES are predominantly composed of long-chain fatty acids and menthol/thymol derivatives, the ionic class can be classified into zwitterionic and halogen-containing types. Given the unique structural variations of NADES, the two components of zwitterionic DESs were carefully chosen to represent combinations popularly employed in extractions, catalysis, and organic synthesis, as shown in Figure 1. Even though some eutectic mixtures may deviate significantly from the eutectic point,40 HBA and HBD combinations examined in this work have been described as DESs in previous studies;16,22,41 they are being referred to as DESs for the sake of simplicity. Most DESs comprised the [Bet] HBA, as it offered the closest resemblance to the [Ch⁺][Cl-] salt by substituting the hydroxyl functional group with a carboxylate substituent, which also acts as the primary hydrogen bond base in the zwitterion. In contrast, the [L-Car] salt incorporates features from the [Bet] and [Ch⁺][Cl-] HBAs by possessing both the hydroxyl and the carboxylate functionalities. The type of hydrogen base alone can significantly influence the solvation properties as [Ch⁺][Cl-] is known to undergo stronger hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl functional group of its cation and chloride anion. In contrast, the [Bet] HBA cannot form strong interactions between its shielded quaternary nitrogen and the carboxylate substituent.20 Additionally, [4-MM-4-oxide] was investigated to elucidate the effect of cyclic zwitterions, while [SB3-14] and [SB3-BIM] were chosen to study the effect of carboxylate and sulfonate moieties. The diverse range of HBDs employed in this study included both straight-chained and branched organic acids and diols. Neat HBDs were also investigated to compare their solvation properties with those of DESs comprising them. In addition, most HBAs and HBDs were mixed together in 2–3 molar ratios to also study the effect of the HBD molar ratio.

3.2. Kamlet–Taft Solvent Parameters. To characterize and quantify unique interactions using the solvatochromic dye approach, all DESs were examined using the Kamlet–Taft solvent parameters. The strength of the HBA is represented by the hydrogen bond basicity, while the hydrogen bond acidity provides a measure of the hydrogen bond-donating ability of the HBD. Table 1 lists the values for the hydrogen bond

donating ability (α), hydrogen bond accepting ability (β), and dipolarity/polarizability (π*). The hydrogen bond donating ability varied between (0.73 ± 0.01) and (1.13 ± 0.02) and was found to be strongly influenced by the type of HBD. The [Bet]/2 Gly and [Bet]/7 Gly DESs offered among the highest α-term values of (1.11 ± 0.01) and (1.13 ± 0.02), respectively, while both the [Bet]/7 TEG and [4-MM-4-oxide]/PheAceA DESs possessed the lowest hydrogen bond donating ability of (0.73 ± 0.02). A comparison of the [Bet]/7 (1,4-BD) (0.86 ± 0.01), [Bet]/7 (1,2-PD) (0.83 ± 0.02), and [Bet]/7 LvA (0.92 ± 0.01) DESs revealed that those composed of organic acid-based HBDs generally offered higher hydrogen bond donating ability, while 1,4-BD resulted in slightly higher α-term values in relation to 1,2-PD. Unlike diols, the α-term was observed to vary significantly for DESs composed of organic acids when the molar ratio of HBD was varied, as respective values of (0.81 ± 0.01), (0.87 ± 0.02), and (0.92 ± 0.01) were obtained for the [Bet]/3 LvA, [Bet]/5 LvA, [Bet]/7 LvA DESs. Additionally, the [SB3-14] HBA was found to possess the highest hydrogen bond donating ability with a value of (1.03 ± 0.02) for the [SB3-14]/7 LvA DES compared to the [Bet]/7 LvA (0.92 ± 0.01), [L-Car]/7 LvA (0.94 ± 0.02), and [4-MM-4-oxide]/7 LvA (0.96 ± 0.01) DESs.

## 4. CONCLUSIONS DESs composed of zwitterionic HBAs form a popular class of sustainable solvents. Given that zwitterionic salts can form DESs with a wide variety of HBDs, these solvents possess unique and diverse physicochemical properties due to their amphiphilic nature. While zwitterionic DESs have been employed as solvents or reaction media in catalysis, organic synthesis, and chemical separations, their solvation character-istics have never been thoroughly studied with either the solvatochromic dye method or IGC.

Using the Nile red dye polarity scale, glycerol-based DESs were observed to possess the highest polarity among the DESs examined in this study, while those composed of organic acids were generally more polar than most diols. Studying the same DESs using Kamlet-Taft solvent parameters revealed that DESs composed of glycerol possess stronger hydrogen bond donating ability than most DESs while the α-term varied significantly for those composed of organic acids when the molar ratio of HBD was varied, unlike diols. Additionally, the [SB3-14] HBA was found to offer the highest hydrogen bond donating ability compared to [Bet], [L-Car], and [4-MM-4-oxide] HBAs. Those DESs that exhibited higher hydrogen bond donating ability generally offered lower hydrogen bond accepting and vice versa, while dipolar interactions did not vary drastically when systematic modifications were made to the DES chemical structure. Using the Abraham solvation parameter model, up to five types of unique interactions could be compared for the same DESs, and those composed of sulfobetaine HBAs possessing longer alkyl chains generally exhibited higher hydrogen bond basicity and dispersive-type interactions. Solvation models generated using both the solvatochromic dye approach and IGC were generally in agreement, and it was found that the type of HBD more strongly influenced the solvation interactions of zwitterionic DESs compared to the nature of the HBA. In addition, the solvation interactions of neat HBDs were generally observed to be similar to their DESs only at very high HBA/HBD ratios of 1:7. Results from this study highlight the need to use multiple approaches and polarity scales to elucidate the solvation properties of complex solvents and provide the framework to simultaneously employ IGC and fluorescent dye methods for their complete characterization.

bond acceptor (HBA) that interacts with a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) to yield eutectic mixtures possessing low melting points compared to the HBA and HBD alone. 3,4 While HBAs typically comprise tetraalkylammonium, phosphonium, imidazolium, and choline salts, the choice of HBDs can include organic acids, alcohols, amides, and carbohydrates. 5,6 DESs often possess desirable properties such as tunable viscosities, 7 low vapor pressures, 1,8 and ease of preparation, 1,9 and are preferentially employed in catalysis, 10,11 organic synthesis, 12 chemical separations, 13,14 and electrochemical applications. 15 Several classes of DESs have been established over the years, each possessing unique features and characteristics. ¹ Among these is the zwitterionic class of DESs that are predominantly composed of betaine [Bet] and L-carnitine [L-Car] salts employed as HBAs that offer lower cytotoxicity and do not generate undesirable side products compared to tetraalkylam- monium and choline salts. ¹⁶,¹⁷ It has been reported that halogen counterions can impart strong nucleophilic, alkaline, and oxidizing properties to halide-containing DESs that can severely corrode steel acquired from fossil fuels.²⁰,²¹ Additionally, zwitterionic surfactants possess amphiphilic properties that allow them to form micelle-like assemblies and behave as hydrophilic and hydrophobic Like all other classes of DESs, the polarity of zwitterionic DESs is strongly influenced by the type of HBA and HBD and/or their molar ratio.¹⁸,²⁷,²⁸ In an attempt to understand their molecular interactions, Abranches et al. studied the solid–liquid phase diagrams of betaine-based DESs and found that betaine possesses a charge imbalance and cannot establish strong ion– ion interactions with itself, unlike salts that possess counter- ions.²⁰ Nevertheless, this study did not quantify the individual solvation interactions of these DESs. Conventionally, the solvation properties of DES systems have been investigated by studying their solvatochromic response to construct the betaine dye scale (EₜN).²⁹,³⁰ For example, an EₜN value of 0.36 was obtained for the [Ch⁺][Cl⁻]/glycolic acid DES compared to 0.79 for the [Ch⁺][Cl⁻]/malonic acid DES, thereby revealing their different solvation characteristics.³¹ Given that the EₜN scale is dependent on a single dye measurement, the Kamlet–Taft solvent parameters employ several solvatochromic probes and can measure the solvent's hydrogen bond donating ability (α), hydrogen bond accepting ability (β), and dipolarity/polarizability (π*).³¹,³² While the fluorescence-based probe approach was the first to characterize DES solvation proper- 4085 https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.2c04425 Ind. Eng. Chem. Res. 2023, 62, 4084–4094 Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research pubs.acs.org/IECR Article ties,³³,³⁴ it has failed in some cases to deconvolute these interactions. For example, Kim and co-workers reported a statistically similar EᴛN value of 0.843 for the [Ch⁺][Cl⁻]/ urea/glycerol ternary DES system compared to 0.845 for the [Ch⁺][Cl⁻]/glycerol DES,³⁵ despite significant differences in their chemical structures. Similarly, Pandey et al. obtained EᴛN values of 0.82 for both the [Ch⁺][Cl⁻]/2 ethylene glycol DES and ethylene glycol,³⁶ demonstrating very little difference between the neat HBD and its DES. It has been concluded that the solvatochromic approach is insensitive to DES compositional changes due to their high polarity and is generally more reliable when the solvation properties from two different classes of DESs are compared.³¹,³² In an attempt to enhance the sensitivity in characterizing DES solvation properties, inverse gas chromatography (IGC) has been recently employed to investigate solute-solvent interactions. 34,37 The chromatographic retention of a diverse variety of probe molecules is measured on DES stationary phases as a function of temperature in order to characterize and quantify their unique and simultaneous interactions with DESs. To date, popular DES combinations comprising tetraalkylammonium, phosphonium, and choline salts have been studied using both the IGC38 and the solvatochromic dye approaches. 30,31 While zwitterionic-based DESs composed of different classes of HBDs have been employed in several applications, no study has attempted to thoroughly characterize their individual solvation interactions. Currently, only a few zwitterionic DESs comprising N-oxide HBAs have been screened using the Nile red solvatochromic scale, 22 which only provides a single value for polarity and does not explain all types of unique interactions that the DESs are capable of undergoing. 2 Consequently, the solvation properties of zwitterionic DESs have not been investigated with either Kamlet–Taft parameters or IGC and, thus, cannot be compared to those of other DES classes. In this study, zwitterionic DESs formed by mixing betaine-, L-carnitine, and sulfobetaine-based HBAs with alcohol- and organic acid-based HBDs were characterized for the first time using both the IGC and the solvatochromic dye method. The choice of HBA and HBD was carefully made to incorporate unique functional groups, such as phenyl and imidazolium substituents, while the molar ratio of HBD was systematically modulated to investigate the effect of the HBA/HBD ratio. Additionally, the solvation properties of DESs were bench- marked against neat HBDs that comprise them. Two different solvatochromic scales (Nile red polarity scale and the Kamlet- Taft solvent parameters) were employed to thoroughly characterize the solvation properties of all DESs using solvatochromic dyes. This study demonstrates the need to simultaneously employ multiple types of approaches and empirical polarity scales in order to fully characterize the solvation properties of complex DESs and is the first to thoroughly investigate subtle differences in solvation character- istics between surfactant-like and halide-containing DESs. ## 2. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION ### 2.1. Reagents, Materials, DES Preparation and Characterization. A comprehensive list of reagents and starting materials employed in this study is provided in the Supporting Information. All HBAs and HBDs were thoroughly dried for 48 h in a vacuum oven maintained at 25 °C prior to being employed in DES preparation using the grinding method. Precise quantities of reagents corresponding to desired HBA/HBD ratios (see Figure 1) were weighed into a ceramic mortar using a clean spatula for zwitterionic salts and a transfer pipette for liquid HBDs. Contents of the mortar were ground together with a pestle until a homogeneous liquid was obtained. The newly prepared DESs were transferred into 20 mL glass vials and their purity was characterized using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy prior to further analysis; all ¹³C and ¹H NMR spectra are provided in the Supporting Information. The water content of each DES was found to be under 0.9 wt % (Table S1), as determined using a Metrohm 831 Karl Fischer coulometric titrator by measuring each sample in triplicate. Additionally, DES viscosity measurements were performed at 21.6 °C using an AMETEK Brookfield DV1 cone and plate viscometer (Middleborough, MA, USA) equipped with a CPA-51Z cone spindle and compared to halide-containing DESs that had similar chemical structures; data are provided in Table S2. Thermal properties of DESs were characterized using a NETZSCH DSC 214 Polyma instrument (Selb, Germany). DESs that possessed a liquid consistency at room temperature were cooled from 40 to -120 °C at a rate of 10 °C min⁻¹ and subsequently heated to 80 °C at the same rate, while those that appeared as solids under ambient conditions were cooled to -65 °C at a rate of 10 °C min⁻¹ before reheating them to 200 °C at the same rate. DSC thermograms were analyzed using NETZSCH Proteus software to obtain the melting point and/or glass transition temperatures for all DESs, as shown in Table S3. ## 2.2. Solvatochromic Dye Measurements. To conduct polarity measurements for zwitterionic DESs using the solvatochromic approach, Nile red (NR), 4-nitroaniline (4-NA), and N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline (N,N-DENA) dyes were employed. 29 The NR and N,N-DENA dyes were dissolved in chloroform to prepare 0.01 M stock solutions, while 4-NA was solubilized in methanol at the same concentration. Dye solutions were stored under 4 °C, and 100 µL of each dye was pipetted into clean Eppendorf tubes. The solvent was evaporated by passing a gentle stream of nitrogen, leaving behind pure dyes as residues in the tubes. A 100 µL volume of DESs was placed into the Eppendorf tubes and thoroughly mixed with each of these dyes to fully solubilize them in the eutectic mixtures. A small volume of each DES/dye solution (20 µL) was transferred into a 96-well plate and analyzed using a Synergy H1 microplate reader (Biotek, Winooski, Vermont). Spectral scanning was performed between wavelengths of 300 and 700 nm in 1 nm increments. The maximum absorption wavelength (λmax) was recorded for each dye, and representative UV–Vis spectra can be found in Figure S1 of the Supporting Information. ## 2.3. DES Chromatographic Column Preparation and Characterization. DESs were employed as GC stationary phases using the static method of column preparation. A 32 mg mass of each DES was placed inside a 20 mL glass vial and dissolved in a mixture of dichloromethane/methanol (up to 5% methanol) to prepare DES coating solutions at a concentration of 0.32% w/v. Five-meter segments of deactivated fused-silica capillary were filled with DES coating solutions and sealed at one end using a metal clamp. The other end was connected to a vacuum and placed inside a water bath maintained at 40 °C. The solvent was steadily evaporated, and the DESs were coated onto the inner walls of the silica capillary. All DESs were coated as a uniform film with a thickness of 0.20 μm.39 4086 https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.iecr.2c04425 Ind. Eng. Chem. Inlet/ detector temperatures were maintained at 150 °C, while the GC oven temperature was modulated between 30 and 50 °C. Additionally, the inlet split ratio was maintained at 20:1. Columns that were prepared from DESs composed of 1,2-PD and PheAceA HBDs had both of their ends connected to 10 cm segments of empty fused silica capillary using press-fit column connectors for GC (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, USA), which were then connected to the inlet/detector. Column efficiencies were determined by separating naphtha- lene (1 mg/mL) at 60 °C and were found to vary between 1700 and 3600 plates/m. In addition, probe molecules comprising alcohols, haloalkanes, and nitroalkanes were solubilized in dichloromethane at a concentration of 1000 ppm (1 mg/mL), and 1 µL was injected onto the DES columns. A comprehensive list of 50 probe molecules employed in this study is provided in Table S4. Multiple linear regression analysis (MLRA) and statistical calculations were performed using Analyze-it (Microsoft, USA). ## 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Natural deep eutectic solvents (NADES), which are perceived to be the least toxic and most sustainable class of DESs, can be categorized into ionic and non-ionic. While non-ionic NADES are predominantly composed of long-chain fatty acids and menthol/thymol derivatives, the ionic class can be classified into zwitterionic and halogen-containing types. Given the unique structural variations of NADES, the two components of zwitterionic DESs were carefully chosen to represent combinations popularly employed in extractions, catalysis, and organic synthesis, as shown in Figure 1. Even though some eutectic mixtures may deviate significantly from the eutectic point,40 HBA and HBD combinations examined in this work have been described as DESs in previous studies;16,22,41 they are being referred to as DESs for the sake of simplicity. Most DESs comprised the [Bet] HBA, as it offered the closest resemblance to the [Ch⁺][Cl-] salt by substituting the hydroxyl functional group with a carboxylate substituent, which also acts as the primary hydrogen bond base in the zwitterion. In contrast, the [L-Car] salt incorporates features from the [Bet] and [Ch⁺][Cl-] HBAs by possessing both the hydroxyl and the carboxylate functionalities. The type of hydrogen base alone can significantly influence the solvation properties as [Ch⁺][Cl-] is known to undergo stronger hydrogen bonding between the hydroxyl functional group of its cation and chloride anion. In contrast, the [Bet] HBA cannot form strong interactions between its shielded quaternary nitrogen and the carboxylate substituent.20 Additionally, [4-MM-4-oxide] was investigated to elucidate the effect of cyclic zwitterions, while [SB3-14] and [SB3-BIM] were chosen to study the effect of carboxylate and sulfonate moieties. The diverse range of HBDs employed in this study included both straight-chained and branched organic acids and diols. Neat HBDs were also investigated to compare their solvation properties with those of DESs comprising them. In addition, most HBAs and HBDs were mixed together in 2–3 molar ratios to also study the effect of the HBD molar ratio. 3.1. Nile Red Dye Polarity Scale (E$_{NR}$). DESs that generally offered higher hydrogen bond donating ability exhibited the lowest β-term values. Due to the strong dependence on pKa, organic acid-based DESs possessed much lower hydrogen bond accepting ability compared to those composed of diols, as observed from β-term values of (0.43 ± 0.01), (0.29 ± 0.01), and (0.61 ± 0.01) for the [Bet]/5 (1,4-BD), [Bet]/5 LvA, and [Bet]/5 (1,2-PD) DESs, respectively. A comparison of diol-based DESs revealed that those composed of 1,2-PD offered much higher hydrogen bond accepting ability than those formed with 1,4-BD. Additionally, values for the β-term did not vary significantly when the molar ratio of HBD was varied, regardless of the HBD. The nature of HBA appeared to drastically influence the hydrogen bond accepting ability, as observed by comparing the β-term values of the [SB3-14]:7 LvA (0.49 ± 0.02), [Bet]/7 LvA (0.27 ± 0.01), [L-Car]/7 LvA (0.39 ± 0.01), and [4-MM-4-oxide]/7 LvA (0.42 ± 0.02) DESs. Compared to a previously reported β-term value of 0.554 for the [Ch+][Cl-]/2 Gly DES,31 the [Bet]/2 Gly DES exhibited a slightly lower hydrogen bond accepting ability of (0.49 ± 0.01), demonstrating a key difference between the surfactant-like and halide-containing classes of DES. In addition, the β-term for DESs composed of the isosorbide HBD could not be evaluated as no peak was detected in the UV-Vis wavelength region for the 4-NA dye. The π*-term represents all of the non-specific interactions that the DESs are capable of undergoing, including dipole–dipole and dipole-induced dipole interactions.²⁹ Dipolar interactions were found to range from (0.87 ± 0.01) to (1.17 ± 0.01) and did not vary drastically. The π*-term values for betaine-based DESs composed of LvA, 1,4-BD, and 1,2-PD were found to be statistically similar at all molar ratios of HBD, indicating that the dipolarity/polarizability did not vary significantly between diols and organic acids. However, both of the [Bet]/2 Gly and [Bet]/7 Gly DESs exhibited significantly higher dipolar interactions of (1.16 ± 0.01) and (1.17 ± 0.01), respectively, which can be attributed to a larger number of hydrogen bond donating sites for glycerol compared to diols and LvA.³⁶ While the π*-term values for the [Bet]/7 LvA (1.02 ± 0.01) and [L-Car]/7 LvA (0.98 ± 0.02) DESs were similar, the [SB3-14]:7 LvA DES exhibited a significantly lower value of (0.87 ± 0.01), demonstrating the lower dipolarity/polarizability of sulfobetaine-based DESs. CONCLUSIONS DESs composed of zwitterionic HBAs form a popular class of sustainable solvents. Given that zwitterionic salts can form DESs with a wide variety of HBDs, these solvents possess unique and diverse physicochemical properties due to their amphiphilic nature. While zwitterionic DESs have been employed as solvents or reaction media in catalysis, organic synthesis, and chemical separations, their solvation character-istics have never been thoroughly studied with either the solvatochromic dye method or IGC. Using the Nile red dye polarity scale, glycerol-based DESs were observed to possess the highest polarity among the DESs examined in this study, while those composed of organic acids were generally more polar than most diols. Studying the same DESs using Kamlet-Taft solvent parameters revealed that DESs composed of glycerol possess stronger hydrogen bond donating ability than most DESs while the α-term varied significantly for those composed of organic acids when the molar ratio of HBD was varied, unlike diols. Additionally, the [SB3-14] HBA was found to offer the highest hydrogen bond donating ability compared to [Bet], [L-Car], and [4-MM-4-oxide] HBAs. Those DESs that exhibited higher hydrogen bond donating ability generally offered lower hydrogen bond accepting and vice versa, while dipolar interactions did not vary drastically when systematic modifications were made to the DES chemical structure. Using the Abraham solvation parameter model, up to five types of unique interactions could be compared for the same DESs, and those composed of sulfobetaine HBAs possessing longer alkyl chains generally exhibited higher hydrogen bond basicity and dispersive-type interactions. Solvation models generated using both the solvatochromic dye approach and IGC were generally in agreement, and it was found that the type of HBD more strongly influenced the solvation interactions of zwitterionic DESs compared to the nature of the HBA. In addition, the solvation interactions of neat HBDs were generally observed to be similar to their DESs only at very high HBA/HBD ratios of 1:7. Results from this study highlight the need to use multiple approaches and polarity scales to elucidate the solvation properties of complex solvents and provide the framework to simultaneously employ IGC and fluorescent dye methods for their complete characterization. ◼ ASSOCIATED CONTENT ⑤ Supporting Information The Supporting Information is available free of charge at https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.iecr.2c04425. EXPERIMENTAL SECTION ### 2.1. Reagents, Materials, DES Preparation and Characterization. A comprehensive list of reagents and starting materials employed in this study is provided in the Supporting Information. All HBAs and HBDs were thoroughly dried for 48 h in a vacuum oven maintained at 25 °C prior to being employed in DES preparation using the grinding method. Precise quantities of reagents corresponding to desired HBA/HBD ratios (see Figure 1) were weighed into a ceramic mortar using a clean spatula for zwitterionic salts and a transfer pipette for liquid HBDs. Contents of the mortar were ground together with a pestle until a homogeneous liquid was obtained. The newly prepared DESs were transferred into 20 mL glass vials and their purity was characterized using nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy prior to further analysis; all ¹³C and ¹H NMR spectra are provided in the Supporting Information. The water content of each DES was found to be under 0.9 wt % (Table S1), as determined using a Metrohm 831 Karl Fischer coulometric titrator by measuring each sample in triplicate. Thermal properties of DESs were characterized using a NETZSCH DSC 214 Polyma instrument (Selb, Germany). CONCLUSIONS DESs composed of zwitterionic HBAs form a popular class of sustainable solvents. Given that zwitterionic salts can form DESs with a wide variety of HBDs, these solvents possess unique and diverse physicochemical properties due to their amphiphilic nature. While zwitterionic DESs have been employed as solvents or reaction media in catalysis, organic synthesis, and chemical separations, their solvation character-istics have never been thoroughly studied with either the solvatochromic dye method or IGC. Using the Nile red dye polarity scale, glycerol-based DESs were observed to possess the highest polarity among the DESs examined in this study, while those composed of organic acids were generally more polar than most diols. Studying the same DESs using Kamlet-Taft solvent parameters revealed that DESs composed of glycerol possess stronger hydrogen bond donating ability than most DESs while the α-term varied significantly for those composed of organic acids when the molar ratio of HBD was varied, unlike diols. Additionally, the [SB3-14] HBA was found to offer the highest hydrogen bond donating ability compared to [Bet], [L-Car], and [4-MM-4-oxide] HBAs. Those DESs that exhibited higher hydrogen bond donating ability generally offered lower hydrogen bond accepting and vice versa, while dipolar interactions did not vary drastically when systematic modifications were made to the DES chemical structure. Using the Abraham solvation parameter model, up to five types of unique interactions could be compared for the same DESs, and those composed of sulfobetaine HBAs possessing longer alkyl chains generally exhibited higher hydrogen bond basicity and dispersive-type interactions. Solvation models generated using both the solvatochromic dye approach and IGC were generally in agreement, and it was found that the type of HBD more strongly influenced the solvation interactions of zwitterionic DESs compared to the nature of the HBA. In addition, the solvation interactions of neat HBDs were generally observed to be similar to their DESs only at very high HBA/HBD ratios of 1:7. Results from this study highlight the need to use multiple approaches and polarity scales to elucidate the solvation properties of complex solvents and provide the framework to simultaneously employ IGC and fluorescent dye methods for their complete characterization. ◼ ASSOCIATED CONTENT ⑤ Supporting Information The Supporting Information is available free of charge at https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.iecr.2c04425.
